questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Trace feeding relationships and explain how biological processes move carbon.
questions.prompt: In a school garden, caterpillars eat okra leaves, and lizards eat the caterpillars. Write the food chain with arrows and explain what an arrow means.
questions.answer: Okra → caterpillar → lizard. Each arrow points from the food to its consumer, showing the direction of transfer of energy.

markingGuide.description: Put all three organisms in feeding order.
Draw both arrows pointing towards the consumer.
Explain the direction of energy transfer.

questions.explanation: Put all three organisms in feeding order. Draw both arrows pointing towards the consumer. Explain the direction of energy transfer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Trace feeding relationships and explain how biological processes move carbon.
questions.prompt: Fungi decompose a pile of dead leaves. Explain how some carbon from the leaves can enter the air and later become part of a living seedling.
questions.answer: Decomposers use organic compounds from the leaves and release carbon dioxide by respiration. A seedling takes in carbon dioxide and uses its carbon to build organic compounds during photosynthesis.

markingGuide.description: Link decomposition to the use of carbon compounds in the leaves.
Identify respiratory release of carbon dioxide.
Explain uptake and fixation by photosynthesis.

questions.explanation: Link decomposition to the use of carbon compounds in the leaves. Identify respiratory release of carbon dioxide. Explain uptake and fixation by photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Trace feeding relationships and explain how biological processes move carbon.
questions.prompt: An observer says a fall in the number of frogs after a fall in insect numbers proves that food shortage caused the change. Explain why this conclusion is uncertain and identify one additional observation that would help test it.
questions.answer: The pattern is consistent with less food, but a third factor could affect both populations. For example, compare frog numbers in similar sites with and without the insect decline while recording habitat conditions.

markingGuide.description: Distinguish association from proof of causation.
Give a plausible alternative factor or explanation.
Suggest a relevant comparison or observation.

questions.explanation: Distinguish association from proof of causation. Give a plausible alternative factor or explanation. Suggest a relevant comparison or observation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Trace feeding relationships and explain how biological processes move carbon.
questions.prompt: In a pond, algae are eaten by snails, and snails are eaten by fish. Which organism is the primary consumer in this chain?
options: The alga
The snail
The fish
A fungus decomposing dead fish
questions.explanation: The snail feeds directly on a producer.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Trace feeding relationships and explain how biological processes move carbon.
questions.prompt: Some energy in a grasshopper’s food never reaches the bird that eats it. Which process accounts for part of that difference?
questions.answer: The grasshopper uses energy in respiration and transfers some to its surroundings as heat.
options: The grasshopper uses energy in respiration and transfers some to its surroundings as heat.
The grasshopper absorbs all of the food into new body tissue.
The bird gives energy back to the grasshopper when it feeds.
The food contains no energy until the bird eats the grasshopper.
questions.explanation: Energy used in the grasshopper’s life processes is unavailable as chemical energy in the tissue eaten by the bird.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Trace feeding relationships and explain how biological processes move carbon.
questions.prompt: Which process directly removes carbon dioxide from the air and incorporates its carbon into plant sugars?
options: Respiration
Combustion
Transpiration
Photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes carbon from carbon dioxide into organic compounds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Relate leaf features to photosynthesis and interpret evidence about light and gas exchange.
questions.prompt: A leaf has a transparent upper epidermis and many chloroplasts in cells just beneath it. Explain how these features work together during photosynthesis.
questions.answer: The transparent epidermis transmits light. Chlorophyll in chloroplasts below it absorbs light energy used for photosynthesis.

markingGuide.description: Link the upper epidermis to transmission of light.
Locate chloroplasts in the illuminated tissue.
Link chlorophyll to absorption of light energy.

questions.explanation: Link the upper epidermis to transmission of light. Locate chloroplasts in the illuminated tissue. Link chlorophyll to absorption of light energy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Relate leaf features to photosynthesis and interpret evidence about light and gas exchange.
questions.prompt: A pupil tests a leaf for starch after keeping its plant in bright light. The pupil concludes that all starch found must have been made that morning. Give one reason this may be wrong and one improvement.
questions.answer: Some starch could have been present before the morning exposure. First destarch the plant and verify with a baseline leaf test before beginning the light treatment.

markingGuide.description: Suggest destarching or a valid baseline comparison.

questions.explanation: Identify possible pre-existing starch. Suggest destarching or a valid baseline comparison.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Relate leaf features to photosynthesis and interpret evidence about light and gas exchange.
questions.prompt: Under bright light, a healthy leaf takes in more carbon dioxide than it releases. Explain how this can happen even though its cells continue to respire.
questions.answer: Respiration releases carbon dioxide, but photosynthesis consumes it at a higher rate. The net movement is therefore into the leaf.

markingGuide.description: Identify carbon dioxide release by respiration.
Relate the net direction to the difference between rates.

questions.explanation: Identify carbon dioxide release by respiration. Identify consumption by photosynthesis. Relate the net direction to the difference between rates.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Relate leaf features to photosynthesis and interpret evidence about light and gas exchange.
questions.prompt: A leaf is coated on both surfaces with a clear substance that blocks its stomata. Which input to photosynthesis is most directly restricted by blocking the pores?
options: Carbon dioxide
Light
Mineral ions from roots
Chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Stomata allow carbon dioxide to diffuse from the air into the leaf.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Relate leaf features to photosynthesis and interpret evidence about light and gas exchange.
questions.prompt: A previously destarched leaf is exposed to light with one patch covered by opaque paper. The exposed tissue tests positive for starch, while the covered patch does not. Which conclusion is supported?
questions.answer: Light was needed for detectable starch accumulation under these conditions.
options: The covered tissue had no living cells before the test.
The plant respired only in the exposed tissue.
Light supplied the carbon atoms in the starch.
Light was needed for detectable starch accumulation under these conditions.
questions.explanation: The light treatment differed between areas of the same leaf, supporting the role of light in the observed accumulation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.learningObjective: Relate leaf features to photosynthesis and interpret evidence about light and gas exchange.
questions.prompt: Why do air spaces inside a leaf help photosynthesis?
questions.answer: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse from stomata towards photosynthetic cells.
options: They carry dissolved starch directly into the roots.
They prevent gases from reaching the mesophyll.
They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse from stomata towards photosynthetic cells.
They make chloroplasts produce light in darkness.
questions.explanation: Intercellular spaces provide gas diffusion paths within the leaf.
